summary: Italy is part of the Schengen Area: EU citizens travel freely, and Swiss and EEA nationals enter with a valid identity card or passport; nationals of the countries and territories on the EU's visa-exempt list (Annex II of Regulation (EU) 2018/1806) can stay up to 90 days in any 180-day period (the ETIAS travel authorisation is not yet in operation), and nationals of the countries on its visa-required list (Annex I) need a Schengen short-stay visa (standard fee €90 under the Visa Code). The Foreign Ministry's Visa for Italy portal asks four questions to find out whether you need a visa for Italy.

tips.text: The UK FCDO says you need a pass to drive a private or hire car into the historic centre of many Italian cities. The boundaries are usually marked ZTL in black on a yellow background; if you pass the sign, your registration number is likely to be caught on camera and you will be fined if you do not have a pass.

The UK FCDO says many major cities charge a small tourist tax, usually paid at your hotel and unlikely to be included in your booking. The rate varies by city and can depend on the hotel's star rating; hotels often ask for cash, so get a receipt.

The UK FCDO says that if you buy a public transport ticket from a kiosk or machine, you must validate it before you start your journey: officials patrol and issue on-the-spot fines for unvalidated tickets. Some buses and trams accept contactless payment on board.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Italy?
faq.answer: No. The United States is on the EU's visa-exempt list (Annex II of Regulation (EU) 2018/1806), whose nationals can stay up to 90 days in any 180-day period without a visa. Italy is among the countries that will require visa-exempt travellers to have an ETIAS travel authorisation, which is not yet in operation; the official ETIAS website gives the application fee as EUR 20.

faq.question: How much does an Italy Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: The Schengen short-stay visa costs €90 for adults and €45 for children aged six to under 12. Under EU visa facilitation agreements, nationals of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Belarus pay €35 and nationals of Cabo Verde 75% of the standard fee. Italy's Foreign Ministry says a short stay means up to 90 days in any 180-day period, calculated as a single period for all European countries using the EES.

faq.question: Is ETIAS required to enter Italy?
faq.answer: ETIAS is currently not in operation and no applications are being collected; the EU will announce the start date several months before launch. The official ETIAS website gives the application fee as EUR 20.

faq.question: Does Italy have a digital nomad visa?
faq.answer: Italy's Consulate General in London lists a digital nomad visa for the self-employed only and a separate remote worker visa for subordinate workers. For the digital nomad visa it asks for proof of a recognised highly qualified profession; annual income of at least triple the minimum level (€8,500) set for exemption from participation in public health costs; suitable lodging; health insurance covering all hospital and medical costs for the entire stay; and at least six months' work experience in the field; and it says applications may take up to 120 days to process.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Italy without a visa?
faq.answer: Nationals of the countries on the EU's visa-exempt list can stay up to 90 days in any 180-day period, and Italy's Foreign Ministry says this is calculated as a single period for all European countries using the EES. EU law says no entry visa may be imposed on EU citizens; Swiss nationals enter on a valid identity card or passport under the EU–Swiss agreement, and the EEA Agreement incorporates the EU free movement directive.

tips.tourist-tax.text: Many major cities in Italy impose a small tax on tourists. You must usually pay this tax at your hotel as it is unlikely to be included in your holiday booking. The rate of tax varies from city to city and can depend on the star rating of the hotel. Hotels often ask for payment in cash. Make sure you get a receipt.

tips.validate-tickets.text: If you buy a ticket from a kiosk or machine, you must validate it on public transport before you start your journey. Officials patrol public transport and will issue an on-the-spot fine if you do not have a validated ticket. Some buses and trams accept onboard contactless payment.

tips.ztl-zones.text: You need a pass to drive into the historic centre of many Italian cities in a private or hire car. You can buy a pass from most car hire companies. The boundaries are usually marked with the letters ZTL in black on a yellow background. If you pass this sign, your registration number is likely to be caught on camera and you will be fined if you do not have a pass.
